title: The Letter I Almost Didn't Send to My Brother
script: Narrator: [warmly] My brother and I stopped talking three years ago, after an argument about our father's business that neither of us handled well.
Narrator: We said things that night that we probably didn't fully mean, but once the words left our mouths, we couldn't take them back.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Because we were both stubborn, neither of us called first, so the silence just continued, month after month, without either of us really deciding it should.
Narrator: Whenever our mother mentioned his name at dinner, I would change the subject quickly, because I wasn't ready to talk about him yet.
Narrator: [carefully] Although I missed him, admitting that felt like losing an argument I was still convinced I had won.
Narrator: Then, last month, our mother got sick, and suddenly none of that old argument seemed important anymore.
Narrator: [reflective] I sat by her hospital bed and thought about how quickly a family can shrink, without anyone properly noticing until it happens.
Narrator: So I wrote my brother a letter, because calling felt too sudden, and I was afraid I would lose my courage halfway through a phone call.
Narrator: [gently] I apologized for the cruel words and the long silence. I did not use the apology to demand that he accept my view of the business.
Narrator: I almost didn't send it. I actually left it on my desk for four days, reading it again each morning before work.
Narrator: [honestly] When I finally sent it, he replied within an hour, saying he had written something similar that he never had the courage to send either.
Narrator: We met at our mother's hospital room the next day, and although the conversation was awkward at first, we both cried a little, and that helped.
Narrator: [encouraging] We talk weekly now. We agreed to review the business records separately and use a neutral adviser if the dispute becomes difficult again.
Narrator: I learned that pride can prolong harm. Reconciliation needs humility, while real financial disagreements still need a fair and careful process.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator and his brother stop talking three years ago?
options: A disagreement about their father's business
A fight over money he borrowed
A disagreement about their mother's health
quiz.explanation: They stopped talking after an argument about their father's business that neither handled well.

quiz.question: What happened last month that changed the narrator's mind?
options: He moved to a new city
quiz.explanation: Their mother got sick, and suddenly the old argument stopped seeming important to him.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator choose to write a letter instead of calling?
options: Calling felt too sudden and he feared losing his courage
quiz.explanation: He says calling felt too sudden, and he was afraid he would lose his courage halfway through a call.

quiz.question: How long did the letter sit on his desk before he sent it?
quiz.explanation: He left the letter on his desk for four days, reading it again each morning.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude about the argument at the end?
options: It was completely his brother's fault
Pride kept it alive longer than it deserved
quiz.explanation: He concludes some arguments only feel important because pride keeps them alive longer than they deserve.

quiz.question: What kept the brothers apart after the argument?
options: Pride and neither person making the first contact
quiz.explanation: The distance continued without a deliberate decision.

quiz.question: Why does the narrator choose a letter?
options: His mother writes it for him
It lets him speak carefully without losing courage
quiz.explanation: The format supports a difficult first step.

quiz.question: What makes the apology responsible?
options: He names his hurtful words without demanding immediate agreement
He says the whole dispute was unimportant
He asks his brother to apologize first
quiz.explanation: An apology owns conduct rather than bargaining.

quiz.question: How will they handle the business disagreement?
options: Let their mother decide from hospital
Discuss it separately with records and a neutral adviser if needed
quiz.explanation: Reconciliation does not remove practical accountability.

quiz.question: What changes most by the end?
options: They restore regular contact while accepting that disagreement remains
quiz.explanation: The relationship improves without a false perfect ending.
